interest: Central American leaders playing Japanese overtures against U.S. canal fears.
overview: This file (decimal file 894.20217, spanning 1932 to 1940) documents U.S. State Department and Naval Intelligence investigations into suspected Japanese espionage, covert hydrographic surveying, economic infiltration, and propaganda in Nicaragua and adjacent Central American republics. Initiated in 1932 by a confidential circular from Assistant Secretary of State Francis White regarding Japanese individuals disguised as fishermen conducting coastal surveys, the records focus heavily on a November 1935 incident in the Gulf of Fonseca where a Japanese motor vessel fled after being boarded by the Nicaraguan Guardia Nacional near the proposed Bryan-Chamorro naval base site. Subsequent despatches, military intelligence memoranda, and clippings from 1936 to 1940 monitor Japanese efforts to gain influence under President Anastasio Somoza, including subsidized diplomatic visits, attempts to purchase 150,000 hectares along the San Juan River near the projected Nicaragua Canal route, promotional schemes for cotton and banana cultivation involving former Costa Rican minister Raúl Gurdían, public controversies in the Central American press, and commercial surveillance of Japanese residents and trading firms in Managua and Corinto.
